body.text: Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, is once again at the heart of a pollution controversy. Firecrackers burst to celebrate the occasion, one of India’s biggest festivals, shot up air and noise pollution levels across the country, especially in vast swathes of northern India.

On the night of Diwali, the average Air Quality Index (AQI) in New Delhi, the national capital, stood at 376, which falls in the “very poor” bracket as per the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)’s standards. It was the highest Diwali-day reading since 2021. The following day was no better. The Index exceeded the 400 mark in parts of Delhi, pushing pollution levels into the “severe” category.

A similar story unfolded in other Indian cities. A live ranking published by AQI.in on November 9 placed 90 Indian cities among the world’s 100 most polluted. At 6 p.m. on November 9, North Indian cities dominated the list — 43 of the top 50 were from northern India.

Meanwhile, Delhi’s pollution data itself became controversial. At midnight on November 8, monitoring stations were not reporting readings; at 1 am on November 9, 36 stations were not reporting, according to an analysis of CPCB data by the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a nonprofit think tank based in New Delhi.

The missing data do not, by themselves, prove deliberate manipulation; they, however, do raise legitimate questions about the reliability and completeness of the official record during peak pollution hours. Experts have alleged that this created a data gap in pollution measurement.

Anumita Roychowdhury, executive director of a New Delhi-based non-profit, the Center for Science and Environment (CSE), described the “data eclipse precisely during peak Diwali pollution” as “inexplicable.” She highlighted that substantial public funds have been invested in establishing Delhi-National Capital Region (NCR)’s air quality monitoring network — the densest in the country — which is further backed by active operation and maintenance contracts.

Diwali-related air pollution has remained an intensely debated issue in India. One group calls for restrictions and responsible celebration without affecting others. For people with respiratory and cardiac conditions, infants, older people, and even pet owners, the festival can mean a night of toxic air, explosive noise, and considerable distress.

Another group tries to shut down these critics by branding them as anti-tradition and hostile toward Hindu culture. They decry regulations as an attempt to police religious celebration. They ask why such a hue and cry goes missing when crackers are used for Christmas, New Year, or global sports and entertainment events; or over pollution from vehicles and factories.
These traditionalists, who often include senior politicians of India’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), have presented the use of firecrackers as part of the freedom to celebrate the festival.

For instance, in October 2025, Delhi BJP president Virendra Sachdeva said that it was because Delhi had a “Sanatan government” that residents got the opportunity to celebrate Diwali with crackers. The BJP, a Hindu nationalist party, refers to Hindus as Sanatanis. This year, in the eastern state of West Bengal, amid severe air pollution in the state capital of Kolkata, the state’s BJP Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari said only communists and non-Sanatanis complained about firecrackers.

True, Diwali is just one factor in North India’s poor air quality. During this time of the year, weather, transport emissions, stubble burning, and other sources also contribute to the air pollution. Fireworks, nevertheless, add a concentrated pollution burden. The failure to enforce restrictions compounds it.
Besides, the issue is evidently not the celebration of Diwali, but the assumption that its observance must involve fireworks, whatever the cost to others.

Diwali has been celebrated with lamps for centuries, long before gunpowder arrived in India sometime in the 14th or 16th century. Even after gunpowder’s arrival, celebrations with fireworks remained limited to royals and elites.

Mass market production, which allowed firecrackers to be part of public festivities, started barely a century ago. The industry expanded in the decades after Independence, as production, distribution, and affordability increased. Over the past few decades, firecrackers have become an increasingly visible feature of urban and middle-class Diwali celebrations.

Now, for many, Diwali and firecrackers have become synonymous. As a result, on and after Diwali night, many people complain of health difficulties due to choking air and explosive noise: anxiety, breathing difficulties, and heart problems, among others.

Firecrackers release fine particulate matter, including PM2.5, which can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, along with gases and metallic compounds. Exposure can aggravate asthma and other respiratory and cardiovascular conditions. Children, older people, pregnant women, and those with existing illnesses are particularly vulnerable.

There are restrictions on the use of firecrackers. Under India’s Noise Pollution Rules, the permissible ambient noise level in residential areas is 55 decibels during the day and 45 at night (10 p.m. to 6 a.m.). The rules prohibit the bursting of sound-emitting firecrackers during these hours and in designated silence zones. Yet the familiar practice of bursting crackers late into the night routinely raises questions about enforcement.

The debate has reached the courts several times. On October 29, 2026, the Supreme Court permitted certified green firecrackers in Delhi-NCR for November 7 and 8, within restricted time slots: 6–7 a.m. and 8–10 p.m. Fireworks within 300 meters of hospitals, nursing homes, old-age homes, educational institutions and notified silence zones remained prohibited.

“Green crackers” are not pollution-free; they are simply less polluting. Apparently, the court’s approach of allowing their regulated use sought to balance religious and cultural practice with public health. Nevertheless, firecrackers continued to be used much before and after the court-allowed period. Evidently, many do not care about causing distress to others or abiding by the regulations.
The fact remains that millions already mark the occasion without explosive fireworks. They include not only the rich who can afford to buy firecrackers but also the poor who cannot.
